lead: An RF power amplifier is the last active block before the antenna. It must deliver watts, not microwatts, while staying linear enough for the modulation. The design problem is a trade: the most linear classes waste DC power as heat, and the most efficient classes distort the signal and splatter energy into neighbouring channels. Class choice, load matching, back-off and linearization set output power, battery life and spectral mask. Handsets, Wi-Fi routers, cell towers and radar transmitters all depend on this trade.
prereq: You need: 5.3 for compression and IM3, and 5.5 for the transmitter chain.

blocks.text: The transistor is biased at a DC operating point. The conduction angle is the part of one RF cycle, measured in degrees, during which drain current flows. It sets the class. Class A conducts for 360°: the device is always on, quiescent current is large, and the waveform stays close to a scaled copy of the input. Class B conducts for 180°; two devices in push-pull cover the full cycle. Class AB sits between 180° and 360°. Class C conducts for less than 180°, so it is nonlinear but efficient. Classes D, E and F switch the transistor hard on and off; output filtering removes harmonics.

blocks.where: η<sub>D</sub> is drain efficiency in percent; P<sub>RF,out</sub> is RF output power in W; P<sub>DC</sub> is DC supply power in W.
PAE is power-added efficiency in percent; P<sub>RF,in</sub> is RF input drive power in W. PAE subtracts drive power and is always lower than drain efficiency.

blocks.text: The table gives ideal maxima. Real parts lose a few points to knee voltage, on-resistance and matching loss.

At maximum output the drain current swings from near zero to I<sub>max</sub>, and in a choke-fed Class A stage the drain voltage swings from the knee voltage V<sub>knee</sub> up to about 2V<sub>DD</sub> − V<sub>knee</sub>. The load line is the straight line between these limits on the output I–V plane. Its slope is 1/R<sub>opt</sub>, where R<sub>opt</sub> is the optimum load resistance. For Class A, R<sub>opt</sub> ≈ 2(V<sub>DD</sub> − V<sub>knee</sub>) / I<sub>max</sub>. The quiescent current is about I<sub>DC</sub> = I<sub>max</sub>/2, so the same result reads R<sub>opt</sub> ≈ (V<sub>DD</sub> − V<sub>knee</sub>) / I<sub>DC</sub>. The matching network transforms the 50 Ω antenna or filter load to R<sub>opt</sub>. Too low R<sub>opt</sub> wastes current; too high R<sub>opt</sub> clips the drain voltage and compresses the gain.

blocks.where: BO is back-off in dB; P<sub>sat</sub> is saturated output power in W; P<sub>avg</sub> is average output power in W.

blocks.text: Back-off is how far average output sits below saturated output. A modulated signal with high peak-to-average power ratio (PAPR) must back off so peaks are not clipped. The two classes fall at different rates. Class A DC current stays fixed, so its drain efficiency follows the power ratio 10<sup>−BO/10</sup>. Class B DC current falls with signal amplitude, so its drain efficiency follows 10<sup>−BO/20</sup>. At 6 dB back-off, Class A drops from 50% to about 12.5%, while Class B drops from 78.5% only to about 39.3%. The average efficiency over a burst is therefore much lower than the peak data-sheet number.

Memory effects are slow changes in the PA response from thermal drift, bias-circuit time constants and transistor trapping. Distortion at one instant depends on earlier envelope values. Memory makes the inverse nonlinearity frequency-dependent, so a static predistorter cannot cancel it.

Modulated signals such as OFDM have high PAPR. A nonlinear PA creates spectral regrowth: energy appears in adjacent channels, raising adjacent-channel leakage ratio (ACLR) and breaking the spectral mask. Linearization reduces this without backing off too far.

Digital predistortion (DPD) is a baseband block before the up-converter. It computes a nonlinear function with memory that approximates the inverse of the PA. A directional coupler samples the PA output; a feedback receiver down-converts it; an adaptation engine compares it with the wanted signal and updates the DPD coefficients. The PA then looks linear up to a higher power and can run closer to saturation.

Doherty: two devices, carrier and peaking. A quarter-wave impedance inverter combines them. At low power the peaking device is off and the carrier sees a higher load, so it reaches voltage swing early and stays efficient. At peaks the peaking device turns on and shares current. Doherty gives high efficiency at 6–10 dB back-off and is common in base stations.

Envelope tracking (ET): a supply modulator makes V<sub>DD</sub> follow the RF envelope. The supply tracks the RF envelope plus a small headroom above V<sub>knee</sub>, so V<sub>DD</sub>(t) − V<sub>out</sub>(t) stays small and dissipation falls. ET suits handsets where battery life matters. Doherty and ET can be combined. All three methods trade complexity and cost for average efficiency.

figure.caption: Drain efficiency against back-off for ideal Class A and Class B. At 6 dB back-off, Class A falls to about 12.5% and Class B to about 39.3%; Class B DC current falls with the signal, so its efficiency drops more slowly.

spec.aria: Drain efficiency versus output back-off for Class A and Class B, showing efficiency falling as the amplifier backs off from maximum power.

examples.question: A Class AB power amplifier has V<sub>DD</sub> = 3.3 V, average DC current I<sub>DC</sub> = 300 mA, RF output power P<sub>RF,out</sub> = 250 mW and RF input power P<sub>RF,in</sub> = 50 mW. Find the DC power, the drain efficiency and the power-added efficiency.
steps: Convert current to amperes: I<sub>DC</sub> = 300 mA = 0.300 A.
DC power: P<sub>DC</sub> = V<sub>DD</sub> × I<sub>DC</sub> = 3.3 V × 0.300 A = 0.99 W.
Drain efficiency: η<sub>D</sub> = P<sub>RF,out</sub> / P<sub>DC</sub> = 0.250 W / 0.99 W = 0.2525 = 25.3%.
RF input power in watts: P<sub>RF,in</sub> = 50 mW = 0.050 W.
PAE = (P<sub>RF,out</sub> − P<sub>RF,in</sub>) / P<sub>DC</sub> = (0.250 W − 0.050 W) / 0.99 W = 0.2020 = 20.2%.
examples.answer: DC power is 0.99 W, drain efficiency is 25.3%, and PAE is 20.2%.
examples.check:
vdd = 3.3
i = 0.300
pout = 0.250
pin = 0.050
pdc = vdd * i
de = 100 * pout / pdc
pae = 100 * (pout - pin) / pdc
print(round(pdc, 2))
print(round(de, 1))
print(round(pae, 1))

traps: Do not quote peak drain efficiency for a modulated signal. At 8–10 dB back-off the average efficiency can be a small fraction of the peak; exam answers must use average power.
Drain efficiency and PAE are not the same. PAE subtracts RF input power; η<sub>D</sub> does not. PAE is always lower, and the drive power can be a large part of a small PA's budget.
Class C maximum efficiency approaches 100% only as output power approaches zero. A real Class C stage at useful output power has lower efficiency and is strongly nonlinear.
Doherty is an analog load-modulation architecture, not a digital algorithm. DPD is the digital correction block. Mixing the two names loses marks.
Back-off in dB is a power ratio: 6 dB means P<sub>avg</sub> is one-quarter of P<sub>sat</sub>, not one-sixth.

quiz.q: Define drain efficiency and PAE. Why is PAE lower?
quiz.a: η<sub>D</sub> = P<sub>RF,out</sub>/P<sub>DC</sub> × 100%. PAE = (P<sub>RF,out</sub> − P<sub>RF,in</sub>)/P<sub>DC</sub> × 100%. PAE subtracts the RF drive power from the output, so it is always lower than drain efficiency.

quiz.q: Why does Class B have a higher maximum drain efficiency than Class A?
quiz.a: Class A conducts for the full 360° cycle and carries quiescent current even with no signal, so DC power is always drawn. Class B conducts for 180° per device and has near-zero quiescent current. With an ideal push-pull load, the maximum drain efficiency rises from 50% to 78.5%.

quiz.q: A PA has V<sub>DD</sub> = 5 V, I<sub>DC</sub> = 0.8 A, P<sub>RF,out</sub> = 2 W and P<sub>RF,in</sub> = 0.2 W. Find P<sub>DC</sub>, drain efficiency and PAE.
A 9 dB PAPR signal uses a Class A PA with 50% peak drain efficiency. Estimate the average drain efficiency at 9 dB back-off and explain why this matters.
quiz.a: η<sub>avg</sub> ≈ 50% × 10<sup>−9/10</sup> = 50% × 0.126 = 6.3%. The PA draws almost full DC power while delivering low average RF power, so most energy becomes heat. Battery life and thermal design suffer even though the peak efficiency looked good.

Spectral regrowth is the spreading of modulated RF energy into adjacent frequency channels caused by PA nonlinearity. It raises ACLR and can violate the spectral mask. Backing off or linearizing the PA reduces it.

quiz.q: Why do memory effects make digital predistortion harder?
quiz.a: Memory effects make the PA output at one instant depend on past envelope values through thermal, bias and trapping time constants. The needed inverse is then frequency-dependent, so a static nonlinearity cannot cancel it. The DPD model must include memory terms and be adapted.

quiz.q: At 6 dB back-off, compute Class B drain efficiency from its 78.5% maximum.
quiz.a: Class B DC current falls with signal amplitude, so η = 78.5% × 10<sup>−6/20</sup> = 78.5% × 0.501 = 39.3%, about 39.3%.

beyond: Not for the exam. Gallium nitride (GaN) PAs now dominate base stations and radar because of high breakdown voltage and power density. 5G mmWave arrays put a PA behind every antenna element, so efficiency and heat per element matter. Load-pull measurement and X-parameter models are used to design matching. Search for envelope tracking supply modulators, Doherty load modulation, and digital predistortion with memory polynomials.
